source: QC & UX audit of the live build, 2026-08-23 · extended for Caney 2.0, 2026-09-09

tickets.title: Fail closed when the build day is not the reader’s day
tickets.evidence: The day-identity fix makes a stale page honestly labelled, but its clock-keyed surfaces still render: the now-strip, the fly-matrix current cell, the solunar today card. Those have no valid value on an old build — they are the last surfaces that can still mislead.
done: __rlRelabel already computes DATA.dayShift; when it is non-zero, blank every clock-keyed surface and replace it with “No current reading — this page has not rebuilt since <build>”.
Date-keyed surfaces (generation schedule, outlook, hatch) keep rendering — their data is still true about the day it names.
If the build holds no row for the reader’s today, say so rather than falling back to row 0.
Build stamp gains a fourth level for day-shift, visually distinct from the >12h amber.

tickets.title: Deploy watchdog that does not live inside GitHub Actions
tickets.evidence: Forty-plus consecutive scheduled runs failed in 2–5s and nothing alerted. Any monitor running in Actions shares the failure domain with the thing it is monitoring — that is why two days passed unnoticed.
done: Cloudflare Worker on a cron trigger fetches /status/caney.json and reads the build epoch.
Alerts when age exceeds 3h; alert path must not touch GitHub.
Worker cron triggers are free — no new spend.
Test by pausing the deploy and confirming the alert fires.

tickets.title: Second publisher on a different failure domain
tickets.evidence: One publisher, one billing relationship, one point of failure. A launchd job on the Mac publishes the same artifact through a path GitHub cannot break.
done: ./build.sh && wrangler pages deploy out/ on a launchd interval.
Writes a heartbeat file the FRESH-02 watchdog can read, so a sleeping Mac is distinguishable from a broken script.
Never publishes a build that fails verify.py — same gate as CI.

tickets.title: Last-good data cache for all thirteen rivers
tickets.evidence: Only briefing.py keeps a cache (cache_dam.json). The other twelve rivers build with missing data during an upstream outage and publish it without complaint.
done: Promote the cache-and-fallback pattern into a riverlib helper.
Every generator caches its last good upstream payload and falls back on failure.
The page says it is running on cache, with the age — the Caney pattern.
CI persists all caches, not just the Caney’s.

reconciliation.note: cache_dam.json is Caney-only; the other twelve have no last-good cache.

tickets.title: Freshness probe that tests the live site, not the build
tickets.evidence: verify.py gates the build. During the outage the build never ran, so the gate never had an opinion. Nothing checks the artifact that is actually being served.
done: test/freshness.py fetches the live URL and asserts build age, day-identity plumbing, and that today’s row exists.
Run by the watchdog on a schedule, never by CI.
Exit code drives the alert.

reconciliation.note: test/planner-smoke.mjs probes the live site post-deploy — partially covers it.

tickets.title: Guard against the 60-day scheduled-workflow auto-disable
tickets.evidence: The repo went public on 23 Aug to fix the cost problem. GitHub disables scheduled workflows in public repos after 60 days without repository activity — the same silent-staleness failure, arriving by a different door.
done: Watchdog additionally asserts a scheduled run happened in the last 24h.
Document the 60-day rule in CLAUDE.md next to the deploy notes.
Consider a dated no-op commit as a backstop only if the watchdog proves insufficient.

tickets.title: Service worker so the tool works where it is used
tickets.evidence: No service worker and no manifest. The Caney tailwater has essentially no coverage — the moment you need the arrival times is the moment the page cannot load. Everything is already baked into one self-contained HTML file, so this is unusually cheap.
done: Precache each river page, its status JSON and the map assets on first visit.
Cache-first with background revalidate; a stale hit still shows correct labels thanks to day identity.
Verify with the network genuinely disabled, not just throttled.
Cache version keyed to the build epoch so a new deploy supersedes cleanly.

reconciliation.note: web/sw.js — shell cache-first, plan data network-first.

tickets.title: Manifest and install prompt
tickets.evidence: The page already ships an apple-touch-icon and a theme-color — it was designed to live on a home screen — but there is no manifest, so it installs as a bookmark rather than an app.
done: manifest.webmanifest with name, icons, standalone display, theme colour.
Start URL is the HQ; each river page is a valid entry point.
Verify installability in Chrome and iOS Safari.

reconciliation.note: web/manifest.webmanifest + generated icons; installable.

tickets.title: Offline state and last-synced line
tickets.evidence: With a service worker the page will load offline — and must then be explicit that it is serving cache, or it recreates the staleness problem in a new place.
done: Detect offline; show a persistent line stating the data’s age and that you are offline.
Reuse the build-stamp vocabulary rather than inventing a second one.
Retry and refresh when connectivity returns.

reconciliation.note: Offline banner states the snapshot age and refuses to imply currency.

tickets.title: Bundle Leaflet locally instead of loading it from unpkg
tickets.evidence: Aborting requests to unpkg.com leaves #lmap empty — the map dies completely. The rest of the page survives (5,918 chars still render), which shows the dependency is isolated and therefore easy to remove.
done: Vendor Leaflet CSS+JS into the repo and inline or serve locally.
No runtime dependency on a third-party CDN for anything load-bearing.
A test asserts the map still initialises with external hosts blocked.

reconciliation.note: web/assets/leaflet.js is vendored; test asserts it is not a CDN load.

tickets.title: Fall back to the SVG diagram when tiles will not load
tickets.evidence: Satellite tiles come from ArcGIS and need bandwidth the riverbank does not have. The at-scale SVG river diagram already exists as a toggle — it should become the automatic fallback.
done: Detect tile failure and switch to the diagram view with an explanatory line.
Diagram must carry the same pins, arrival markers and colour coding.
Manual toggle still overrides.

tickets.title: Fix the 54 contrast failures at the token level
tickets.evidence: Measured on rendered nodes on caney.html: 54 elements below WCAG AA. Worst offenders sit at 2.07:1 and 2.21:1 where 4.5:1 is required — including a 23px heading. These are token problems, so a token fix lands everywhere at once.
done: Re-derive --muted and --faint so both clear 4.5:1 on card and ground.
Grade chips, unit-colour legends and the small-caps labels all pass.
Re-run the rendered-node contrast audit; zero failures on all thirteen pages.
Colour is never the only carrier of grade or unit count.

reconciliation.note: Planner palette is AA at token level (axe: 0). The thirteen river pages were NOT re-audited.

tickets.title: Bring 227 tap targets up to 44px
tickets.evidence: 227 of 464 interactive elements are under 44px tall at a 390px viewport — roughly half of everything tappable, on a tool operated one-handed, outdoors, often with cold hands.
done: Every button, chip, tab and select reaches 44px of tappable height.
Where visual density matters, grow the hit area with padding rather than the visual box.
Automated check in the browser suite counts undersized targets and fails above zero.

reconciliation.note: Planner controls are ≥44px and tested. River pages untouched.

tickets.title: Honour prefers-reduced-motion
tickets.evidence: The pages animate — pulsing access pins, a gliding front marker, an auto-advancing time slider — and no stylesheet contains a prefers-reduced-motion query. For a vestibular-sensitive reader the map is actively unpleasant.
done: Single riverlib block disables or reduces every animation under the query.
The play control still works; it just steps rather than glides.
Verified by emulating the preference in Playwright.

reconciliation.note: prefers-reduced-motion honoured in web/assets/app.css only.

tickets.title: Visible focus states throughout
tickets.evidence: No :focus rule exists in any stylesheet. Tabbing through the page is invisible — the craft cards, date picker and access selects are all keyboard-reachable and give no indication of where you are.
done: :focus-visible ring on every interactive element, from a token.
Ring is legible on card, ground and the satellite map.
Tab order verified to follow reading order on Caney and the HQ.

reconciliation.note: focus-visible throughout the planner; river pages untouched.

tickets.title: Announce dynamic updates to screen readers
tickets.evidence: Zero aria-live regions. Moving the time slider, switching craft or changing day rewrites entire panels with no announcement — a screen-reader user gets silence and a changed page.
done: Polite live region announces the resulting state, not the raw event ("Powerboat, tomorrow 8/24, wade until 2:30pm").
Debounced so a slider drag announces once on settle.
Verified with VoiceOver.

reconciliation.note: aria-live on the planner result region; river pages untouched.

tickets.title: Alt text for the ten unlabelled images
tickets.evidence: Ten images render with no alt attribute at desktop, six at mobile.
done: Every informational image gets alt text that states what it shows.
Purely decorative images get alt="" so they are skipped rather than read as filenames.
verify.py fails on any image lacking an alt attribute.

reconciliation.note: Alt text on river-page images is untouched.

tickets.title: Automated accessibility gate in CI
tickets.evidence: Every finding above was found by hand, which means it can silently return. The project already has the pattern for this: verify.py and the day-identity gate exist because manual checks kept regressing.
done: axe-core runs against all thirteen pages in the browser suite.
Serious and critical violations fail the build.
Contrast, tap-target and alt checks fold into it rather than living separately.
Baseline recorded so pre-existing issues do not block unrelated work.

reconciliation.note: axe runs in test/planner.mjs and gates the deploy. 0 violations.

tickets.title: Section navigation for a 7,000px page
tickets.evidence: Caney is 7,019px tall at 390px — around eighteen phone screens — with collapsible sections but no way to jump between them. On the water you want one section, immediately.
done: Sticky section index that reflects the fold state.
Deep links per section so a bookmark can open straight to the generation schedule.
Collapses into the existing sticky day bar rather than adding a third sticky layer.

reconciliation.note: Section nav for long river pages is untouched.

tickets.title: Make the river switcher show that it scrolls
tickets.evidence: Fourteen tabs, roughly six visible at 960px. It scrolls horizontally but nothing indicates that — the fourteenth river is undiscoverable if you do not think to swipe.
done: Edge fade or an explicit control signalling more tabs.
Active tab scrolls into view on load.
Consider grouping by drive time, which is how rivers are actually chosen.

reconciliation.note: Switcher scroll affordance is untouched.

tickets.title: Unique title on every page
tickets.evidence: All three Duck sections emit Duck River · smallmouth. In tabs, history and bookmarks the upper, middle and lower reaches are indistinguishable — and they are genuinely different rivers to fish.
done: Title carries the reach: “Duck · Upper (Columbia) · smallmouth”.
verify.py asserts all fourteen titles are unique.

reconciliation.note: Unique titles: the planner has one; the river pages do not.

tickets.title: Meta description and link previews
tickets.evidence: No page has a meta description. Links shared to a fishing partner unfurl as a bare URL.
done: Per-river description generated from live conditions at build time.
Open Graph and Twitter tags with a build-time preview image.
Absolute canonical URL per page.

reconciliation.note: Meta description: the planner has one; the river pages do not.

tickets.title: Dark mode
tickets.evidence: No prefers-color-scheme anywhere. The solunar card recommends a 3:09am minor feed and the whole product is oriented around dawn — then hands you a pure-white screen in the dark.
done: Full token-level dark palette in riverlib; every page inherits it.
Grade, unit and clarity colours re-derived for the dark ground, not inverted.
Map switches to a dark tile layer or dims the satellite imagery.
Contrast re-validated in both themes.

reconciliation.note: Token-level dark mode on the planner. River pages are still light-only.

tickets.title: Print stylesheet
tickets.evidence: The Atlas Generator exists precisely because people want paper on the boat. The pages themselves print as a wall of collapsed sections and a dead map.
done: Expand folds, drop interactive chrome, keep the schedule and arrival table.
Map prints as the diagram rather than a blank tile grid.
Fits legibly on Letter.

reconciliation.note: A print stylesheet exists for the planner only.

tickets.title: Parallelise the build
tickets.evidence: Eleven generators run serially with a hardcoded sleep 2 between them. Measured runs: 135–430s, mean ~279s. CLAUDE.md still says “~30s”, which was true when there was one river.
done: Independent generators run concurrently; hq.py still runs last.
Concurrency tuned so USGS does not rate-limit — the journal already records that failure.
Target under 90s; update the documented figure to the measured one.
A crashed generator still fails the build loudly.

reconciliation.note: planner.py parallelises its own fetches; the generators do not.

tickets.title: Bump the five Node-20 actions
tickets.evidence: Every run warns: checkout, setup-python, cache/restore, cache/save and wrangler-action all target Node 20 and are being force-run on Node 24. It works until it does not.
done: All actions on versions that natively support the current runner.
Warning gone from the run log.

tickets.title: Tighten the job timeout
tickets.evidence: timeout-minutes: 20 against a build that takes two to seven. A hung run burns the full twenty.
done: Timeout set from the measured p99 plus headroom.
Revisit after BUILD-01 lands.

reconciliation.note: Timeout raised to 30 min for the added gates.

tickets.title: De-flake the craft-spread assertion
tickets.evidence: “At least one day grades differently by craft” fails whenever the week’s water is uniform — it failed during this audit for exactly that reason, on a week of identical afternoon releases. A test that fails on legitimate data trains you to ignore failures.
done: Assert the scoring function separates crafts on synthetic inputs, not that this week happens to.
Keep a warning when real data shows no spread — that is information, not a failure.
Suite returns to zero red on a normal week.

tickets.title: Per-generator timing budget
tickets.evidence: Build time tripled as rivers were added and nobody noticed until it was being billed by the minute. The same drift will happen again.
done: Each generator records wall time and upstream fetch count.
Build fails, or warns loudly, when a generator exceeds its budget.
Timings written to the status directory so the trend is visible.

reconciliation.note: out/plan/build.json records planner duration; the generators do not.

tickets.title: Backtest the twelve rivers that have never been validated
tickets.evidence: analysis/backtest_flow.py has only ever run against the Caney — where it moved baseflow 375→205 cfs and leading-edge speed 3.0→2.5 mph, both material corrections to numbers that felt right. Twelve rivers still carry their original, unvalidated constants. This is the largest correctness risk in the product.
done: Run the Caney methodology against every river with sufficient gauge history.
Each river’s constants either confirmed or corrected, with provenance in the comment above them — the existing invariant.
Rivers with insufficient record are marked as such rather than quietly trusted.
Results committed to analysis/ so the next session can see the evidence.

reconciliation.note: The twelve unvalidated rivers are still unvalidated.

tickets.title: Show each river’s model confidence in the interface
tickets.evidence: The Caney’s routing was fitted to r²=0.89; the Cumberland’s is r=0.30 and the page says so only in the footer. The Harpeth’s transfer function beats a constant gain by 3%. A reader cannot tell a measured number from an estimated one.
done: Every river carries a confidence level derived from its backtest, not asserted.
Surfaced next to the prediction it qualifies, not buried in the footer.
Low-confidence rivers state which part is reliable — release schedule versus downstream timing.

reconciliation.note: modelConfidence is on every zone and in the evidence drawer; four separate confidences in 2.1.

tickets.title: Trip log records what the tool predicted
tickets.evidence: The journal calls this the evidence engine, and it is still not built. The log currently captures what you caught; it does not capture what the page said would happen, so it can never grade itself.
done: Every log entry snapshots the prediction: flow, arrival, grade, clarity, data age.
Stored alongside the outcome you record.
Exportable, so a season of it can be analysed offline.

reconciliation.note: trip.js::snapshotPrediction freezes the plan-time state; 2.1 freezes the itinerary, ranking, hourly curves, weights and model versions.

tickets.title: Prediction-versus-observed scoreboard
tickets.evidence: The auto-calibration already compares model to gauge every build (currently ±20 cfs on the Caney) and then throws the comparison away. Kept, it becomes a public accuracy record.
done: Persist the per-build model-versus-gauge residual per river.
A page showing accuracy over time, by river.
Systematic drift triggers a recalibration ticket automatically.

reconciliation.note: The scoreboard answers all of §51: arrival residual, opportunity bands, confidence calibration, per-species, per-zone, itinerary-vs-single-zone, research.

tickets.title: Auto-calibration for the remaining tailwaters
tickets.evidence: Feature 12 in the spec matrix is ✅ for the Caney and ◻ for the Cumberland. The Caney’s auto-calibration measurably tightened the model — the other tailwaters get no such correction.
done: Promote the calibration routine into riverlib.
Enabled on every river with a downstream gauge and a routing model.
Same clamped-median guard, so a bad gauge day cannot swing the page.

reconciliation.note: Auto-calibration is now gated behind the outcome loop rather than a per-river backtest — see docs/OUTCOMES.md. MODEL-01 (#30) is the prerequisite that survives.

tickets.title: Bring the spec matrix up to thirteen rivers
tickets.evidence: §3 has three river columns; the header says “9 rivers”; there are thirteen. The parity rule is enforced by that matrix, so a matrix covering under a quarter of the fleet cannot enforce anything — and the journal has been carrying this as an open thread for weeks.
done: Matrix generated from the registry rather than hand-maintained.
Every ✅ / ◻ / — is machine-checkable against the built pages.
verify.py fails when a page contradicts its own matrix row.

reconciliation.note: The §3 matrix still lists 3 of 13 rivers.

tickets.title: Finish the shared-CSS extraction
tickets.evidence: The last open item in the §5 migration backlog: base design CSS is still duplicated per page. This is the exact condition that broke the Caney hatch calendar — a leftover generic .hatch class colliding with a shared component.
done: Base tokens and layout CSS live in riverlib and are injected once.
No page defines a class name a shared component also uses.
verify.py fails on duplicate class definitions across the shared and per-page layers.

reconciliation.note: One shared stylesheet and shared ES modules for the planner. The generators still inline their own CSS.

tickets.title: Visual regression snapshots
tickets.evidence: The hatch-calendar collision rendered a shattered grid and passed every automated check, because nothing looks at the page. It was found by eye, late.
done: Per-page screenshots at 390 and 1280px, both themes once dark mode lands.
Diffs surfaced in CI; intentional changes accepted explicitly.
Runs on the built output, not on isolated component fixtures — that is what hid the collision.

tickets.title: Scaffold a new river from the registry
tickets.evidence: Thirteen rivers exist and each was cloned from a predecessor. That is how the Buffalo shipped the Duck’s ramp names in its flow timer — a real bug caught only when a later river was added.
done: One command generates a working generator from a registry entry.
Scaffold includes the parity checklist and fails until every item is addressed or justified.
No river-specific place names can survive the clone.

tickets.title: Corpus, slicer and Worker — the bot answers from the build
tickets.evidence: Shipped. bot.json (13 rivers, ~22k tokens) plus a deterministic slicer that ships 800–1,500 tokens per question — 93–96% smaller, ~1.4¢ a question. Deployed at riverguide-bot.steven-b9c.workers.dev, webhook registered, 30 tests green.
done: Corpus gated by verify.py so a rename cannot silently empty it.
Slicing proven verbatim — sliced fields are byte-identical to the build.
Safety rules travel inside the payload, not only the system prompt.

tickets.title: Prove the safety guardrail with adversarial questions
tickets.evidence: The bot is instructed to quote generation times and wade windows verbatim or decline. That instruction is untested — the account has no API credit, so not one real answer has been generated. An unverified safety guardrail is the same class of thing as an alarm that has never fired.
done: A suite of adversarial prompts: asking it to round a release time, convert cfs, average a week, infer a wade window for a river with no wade data, and answer about a river not in the corpus.
Every safety-critical number in a reply must appear verbatim in the slice it was given.
Run against the live bot, not a mock; record the transcript in the repo.
Any failure tightens the system prompt and the test is kept.

reconciliation.note: riverguide/test.mjs drives six adversarial classes against the fail-closed guard.

tickets.title: Cost telemetry — know what a question actually costs
tickets.evidence: 1.4¢ is an estimate from token counts, not an observation. Usage is already metered per chat in KV but nothing reads it back.
done: A /usage command and a health field reporting questions and tokens per day.
Real cost per question by intent, so the free-tier caps in access.js are set from data rather than guessed.
Alert if a day exceeds a spend ceiling.

reconciliation.note: The research worker records queries, tokens and cache hits per day. Bot-side token telemetry already existed.

tickets.title: Open it to anyone — identity, quota, abuse
tickets.evidence: access.js already carries owner/free/paid tiers and OPEN_TO_ALL, and a test proves the flip admits strangers on the free tier. What is missing is everything around it: who they are, what stops abuse, and who pays.
done: An identity story — Claude sign-in or a payment record keyed to the Telegram chat id.
Per-chat and global rate limits, with the global one protecting the API bill.
A cost ceiling that degrades to a static answer from the corpus rather than refusing.
Only then flip OPEN_TO_ALL.

tickets.title: Inline buttons so the bot is discoverable without guessing
tickets.evidence: Free text is the whole interface. A new user has no idea what it knows, and every unparsed question still costs a model call.
done: Telegram inline keyboards for the common asks — what's good now, this week, pick a river.
Button paths answer from the corpus without a model call where the answer is purely lookup.
/start shows them.

tickets.title: Fish it and log trips — the species weights are priors, not calibration
tickets.evidence: Caney 2.0 ships a published weight table per species (docs/SPECIES_SCORING.md) taken straight from the design brief. Nothing has validated a single number in it. The scoreboard that would validate them (web/planner/trip.js) is built and reports water-arrival residual, score-vs-rating correlation, species hit rate and confidence calibration — and currently has zero trips in it. Every other calibration ticket is gated on this one.
done: Twenty logged plans with outcomes recorded, across at least three species.
The scoreboard prints a figure for the arrival residual instead of “not enough trips to say”.
Any weight moved as a result carries its evidence in the comment above it, per the calibration-provenance invariant.

tickets.title: Verify the zone coordinates outside the Caney and Cordell Hull
tickets.evidence: Of 17 fishing zones, only the Caney reaches and the Cordell Hull tailwater carry access coordinates verified against an authority (TWRA Boating & Fishing Access layer, USACE LRN). The rest are OSM centreline positions marked verified: false, and the UI and the map both say so — which is honest but is not the same as being right. This is the highest-value data work left.
done: Every AccessPoint either carries a verified source or is removed.
test_zones.py stops needing the unverified branch for the zones it covers.
No zone geometry is a POINT unless a source published that point.

tickets.title: Largemouth is the thinnest part of the zone model
tickets.evidence: The repo's rivers are current-oriented tailwaters and shoal rivers, so the cover/backwater water largemouth actually want is under-represented: cordell_creek_arms and stones_river carry most of it, and almost every largemouth SpeciesProfileRef is heuristic: true. The regression fixture proves cover water CAN outrank current water; it does not prove the zones are the right ones.
done: Sourced habitat evidence for at least three largemouth zones.
Those SpeciesProfileRefs flip to heuristic: false with claim ids.
test_species.test_largemouth_can_win asserts a specific zone rather than a set.

tickets.title: Refresh the live plane without rebuilding the static plane
tickets.evidence: The architecture separates the two (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5) and planner.py already regenerates out/plan/data.json alone in about two seconds against a warm cache. What is missing is a trigger: today the only thing that runs it is the hourly full build, so a plan is at worst an hour stale even though the dataset behind it is cheap to refresh.
done: A workflow that runs planner.py alone on a short schedule and deploys only out/plan/.
The freshness strip distinguishes dataset age from river-page age.
Post-deploy smoke asserts the shorter budget.

tickets.title: Wire the in-plan question box to RiverGuide properly
tickets.evidence: §46's “Ask about this plan…” drawer currently hands the question to Telegram as pre-filled text. The bot already resolves a planning question to the exact FishingPlan (riverguide/src/plan.js), so the round trip works — but the plan the reader is looking at and the plan the bot fetches are matched by species/craft/preset, not by plan id.
done: The drawer passes the plan id, and the bot fetches that plan.
A question about a plan whose window has passed says so rather than answering about a different one.

tickets.title: Verify access coordinates — a dozen zones sit at location confidence 40
tickets.evidence: Caney 2.1 makes geographic confidence first class and charges for it: window utility multiplies by 0.75 + 0.25 x location_confidence, so an unverified zone gives up real ground, and its tactical language is hedged rather than precise. Of 22 zones, only the Caney reaches, the Cordell Hull tailwater and the Carthage confluence carry verified access. Twelve sit at 40/100 and say so in the UI. This is the single highest-value data task in the repo.
done: Every AccessPoint either carries a verified source or is removed.
The zones currently at 40 move to 62 or better.
docs/GEOGRAPHY.md §5's table is rewritten to match.

tickets.title: The utility constants are priors — twenty logged trips is the threshold
tickets.evidence: The whole 2.1 objective (peak/cubic/floor mixture, the duration saturation at 150 minutes, the 0.22-per-minute transition cost, the breadth bonus, the complexity penalty) was chosen so the four mandatory regression scenarios come out as specified. Nothing has validated any of it. The scoreboard answers every question in the brief's §51 and currently prints 'not enough trips to say' to all of them.
done: Twenty logged plans with outcomes, across at least three species.
The arrival-residual and opportunity-band measures print figures.
Any constant moved carries its evidence in the comment above it, and PLANNER_VERSION is bumped.

tickets.title: Deploy the research worker and point CI at it
tickets.evidence: research-worker/ is written, tested (no network needed) and documented, but not deployed: wrangler.toml still carries REPLACE_WITH_D1_ID and REPLACE_WITH_KV_ID. Until it exists the planner runs on the 23 seeded TWRA/TDEC claims, which is a working floor but a static one — the freshness line on every plan reads from stored evidence only.
done: D1 and KV created, schema applied, OPENAI_API_KEY set as a secret.
/health returns enabled: true.
The CANEY_RESEARCH_ENDPOINT repository variable is set and a build shows research on.

tickets.title: The transition model is priors too — and it decides whether you move
tickets.evidence: caney/planner/transitions.py holds sixteen configured routes and estimates the rest from straight-line distance times a sinuosity factor. Speeds (18 mph downstream in a boat, 32 mph on county roads) and the 14-minute trailering overhead are guesses. They directly decide whether a move is worth making, which is the most consequential new behaviour in 2.1.
done: Time an actual Cordell Hull to Caney mouth run and a trailer reposition.
Replace the two speeds that matter with measured ones.
Segment outcomes confirm the move was worth it, or the cost goes up.

tickets.title: The river pages never got the accessibility or dark-mode work
tickets.evidence: S12-S16 and S23 were delivered on the planner, which is a different surface with its own stylesheet. The thirteen generated river pages still inline their own CSS, are light-only, and have not been through axe. They are now the drill-down layer rather than the front door, which lowers the priority but does not remove it.
done: riverlib's shared CSS adopts the planner's token palette.
axe runs against a river page in CI.
Dark mode works on a river page.

findings: No service worker, no manifest. This is a phone tool for places with no bars.
Blocking unpkg leaves #lmap empty. The rest of the page survives — 5,918 chars still render.
On caney.html alone. Worst 2.07:1 and 2.21:1 against a 4.5:1 requirement.
analysis/backtest_flow.py has only ever run against the Caney. Twelve rivers ship unvalidated constants.
Under 44px tall at a 390px viewport — about half of everything tappable.
Only briefing.py keeps cache_dam.json. The other twelve build empty during an upstream outage.
CSS keyframes present (pulsing pins, gliding front marker); no prefers-reduced-motion query anywhere.
No :focus rule in any stylesheet. Keyboard navigation is invisible.
All three Duck sections share Duck River · smallmouth — indistinguishable in tabs, history, bookmarks.
About eighteen phone screens of Caney, with no section nav to jump between them.
The slider, craft toggle and date picker rewrite whole panels silently.
No prefers-color-scheme anywhere. A pure-white page read at 5am on the water.
Eleven generators serial with a hardcoded sleep 2. Docs still claim ~30s.
§3 has three river columns and the header says “9 rivers”. There are thirteen.
Ten images carry no alt attribute at desktop, six at mobile.
Across all three viewports, including with the CDN blocked.
A build staled two days degrades to “Fri · 2d ago” instead of claiming “Today”.
method: Measured against the live build on 23 Aug 2026 — every page loaded in headless Chromium at 390 / 768 / 1280px, contrast computed per rendered node against its resolved background, CDN failure simulated by aborting unpkg, arcgisonline and the font hosts, overflow measured as scrollWidth > clientWidth.

release.name: Caney 2.1 — the fishing-day oracle
release.summary: The planner stopped optimising the mean. It now finds the best contiguous opportunity WINDOW inside your availability, and assembles the best executable itinerary from those windows — including moving between zones when that is worth the travel. Geographic confidence became first class, research became a refreshable service, and the outcome loop became the point rather than a footnote.
release.addresses: Every ticket below now carries a `reconciliation` block classifying it against what 2.0 and 2.1 shipped: completed, partial, superseded or still relevant. The GitHub issue remains the system of record for whether a ticket is closed — nothing here closes one.
